desc: Beginning the evening of 6 December 2023, unidentified unmanned aircraft operated over Joint Base Langley-Eustis, home of front-line F-22 Raptors, and continued through the month. The Air Force confirmed 'The installation first observed UAS activities the evening of December 6 [2023] and experienced multiple incursions throughout the month of December,' that the drones 'ranged in size/configuration' and that 'the number of UASs fluctuated.' The response is the measure of how seriously it was taken: F-16 combat air patrols with aerial refueling in mid-December, NASA's WB-57F high-altitude research aircraft flying surveillance orbits, FBI coordination through NORTHCOM, and FAA notification. Gen. Mark Kelly told the Wall Street Journal at least one drone was roughly 20 feet long, flying at more than 100 mph at 3,000 to 4,000 feet. The Air Force declined to describe operational impact 'to protect operational security'; F-22s were relocated and protective netting for the aircraft was later considered. Gen. Gregory Guillot, taking NORAD/NORTHCOM command in February 2024, made counter-UAS the centrepiece of his 90-day assessment with Langley as the driving case, and stated flatly that he knew of 'any organized or unorganized foreign nexus.' Seventeen nights of unidentified aircraft over a stealth fighter base, and no attribution has ever been made public.

connections: Gen. Glen VanHerck - NORAD/NORTHCOM commander during the incursions; ordered the F-22 shootdown of the Chinese surveillance balloon ten months earlier; the only four-star to publicly reject the hobbyist explanation; his 16 December 2021 warning to SecDef Lloyd Austin about lack of domain awareness predates Langley by two years and establishes documented foreknowledge of the vulnerability.

Gen. Gregory Guillot - VanHerck's successor from February 2024; made the first public acknowledgment before the Senate Armed Services Committee on 14 March 2024 and made Langley the centerpiece of his 90-day assessment; directed in November 2024 to serve as DoD's synchronizer, integrator and coordinator of counter-small-UAS activity within the continental United States and Alaska; the official through whom nearly all subsequent government characterization of Langley flows.

Gen. Mark Kelly - commander of Air Combat Command, headquartered at Langley; the senior military eyewitness and the source for the WSJ's physical description. Distinct from Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ), SASC and Intelligence Committee member, who separately told reporter Matt Laslo that some base incursions are 'very likely to be foreign nationals that are doing surveillance with low-cost systems that are somewhat expendable.'

AARO (All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office) - reported to have joined two weeks of interagency meetings on Langley, yet told Liberation Times in May 2024 it had received no report; Guillot separately said in October 2024 that he 'coordinates frequently' with AARO. Connects Langley to the board's AARO node and to the pattern of service-level withholding from AARO also alleged of the Navy.

FBI - held jurisdiction outside the base perimeter, received witness video from civilian eyewitness Jonathan Butner, and has declined comment on the investigation since December 2023; the agency in whose files the primary evidentiary record most plausibly sits.

FAA - notified of the incursions; later a signatory to the December 2024 joint statement; the agency whose airspace authority creates the jurisdictional seam VanHerck describes as ending 'at the fence line.'

NASA - the WB-57F N927NA orbits over Langley on 18-19 December 2023 place a civilian science agency's high-altitude imaging asset inside a military anomaly response, with NASA's public explanation (SpaceX CRS-29 support, plus 'additional imaging support in Virginia') covering the tasking.

Chinese surveillance balloon (February 2023) - shot down by an F-22 flown from Langley; the immediately preceding demonstration that NORAD's radar clutter gates were misconfigured for non-traditional aerial objects, and the precedent Guillot cites for 'lessons learned.'

New Jersey / Picatinny Arsenal drone wave (November 2024 onward) - the mass-sighting event that forced the four-agency joint statement and generated the congressional pressure Langley alone had not; the Army confirmed 11 drone sightings over Picatinny Arsenal beginning in November 2024.

Prior and parallel incursion nodes - Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station (2019), the Colorado plains ICBM-field drone reports (winter 2019-2020), the USS Paul Hamilton and other warships off Southern California (2019), Air Force Plant 42 in Palmdale (2024), the Energy Department's Nevada National Security Site nuclear-weapons experiment facility (October 2023), Wright-Patterson AFB, Guam's THAAD battery, and the RAF Lakenheath/Mildenhall/Feltwell cluster in the UK (November 2024).

10 U.S.C. 130i and the 'covered installation' regime - the statutory bottleneck that made non-engagement lawful; Sens. Tom Cotton and Kirsten Gillibrand pushed expansion legislation, and the later Safer Skies Act extended limited mitigation authority to DHS, DOJ, and certain state, local and tribal agencies.

Sen. Roger Wicker - SASC chairman; the ranking legislator to state on camera that the incursions have a military intelligence dimension and that the executive branch remains mystified despite top-level classified briefings.

House Oversight Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs (Chairman William Timmons, Ranking Member Suhas Subramanyam) - the 29 April 2025 'Securing the Skies' hearing, the closest thing to a dedicated congressional examination of the base-incursion pattern.

Fengyun Shi prosecution - the only criminal case to emerge from Hampton Roads airspace in that window, involving a separate January 2024 flight over Newport News Shipbuilding; frequently conflated with the December incursions in secondary coverage and useful chiefly as a control case demonstrating what identification, attribution and prosecution look like when they actually occur.

Joint Base Langley-Eustis ISR units - the 363rd and 480th Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Wings are based at JBLE, meaning the incursions occurred over an installation hosting national-level ISR analytic capability.
Falcon Peak (2024, 2025) - the NORTHCOM-led counter-small-UAS demonstration series at Fort Carson, Colorado, created as a direct downstream product of the Langley assessment.

Ross Coulthart and Liberation Times - the disclosure-side journalists who pressed the eyewitness account and the AARO non-receipt statement into the record; Coulthart has publicly flagged the classification problem, noting that if no craft were ever recovered, the word 'drones' is doing unearned work.
dossier.denialPosture: The government's Langley posture is not denial of the event but denial of its significance, executed through a taxonomy: the objects were declared 'uncrewed aerial systems' without a single one being recovered, downed, tracked, or attributed, which converts an unexplained penetration of restricted airspace into a routine force-protection problem. That posture has four dated, attributable artifacts - the Air Force's 'none of the incursions appeared to exhibit hostile intent' (March 2024), Gen. Guillot's 'I do not know of any organized or unorganized foreign nexus' (October 2024), an unnamed Biden White House official's characterization to 60 Minutes of the affair as likely hobbyists, and the 16 December 2024 four-agency joint statement's 'we have not identified anything anomalous.' It is contradicted on the record by VanHerck, who commanded the response and who says magnitude, size, and duration rule hobbyists out. AARO's May 2024 statement that it had 'not yet received a report or any information on this incident' is the strangest artifact of the set: the office chartered to resolve unidentified objects was, by its own account, never told about the largest unresolved domestic airspace event in decades.
dossier.narrative:
The incursions began after dark on 6 December 2023. A Langley Air Force Base spokesperson, responding to The War Zone three months later, confirmed the outline in language that has never been amended: the installation 'first observed UAS activities the evening of December 6' and 'experienced multiple incursions throughout the month of December,' with the number of objects fluctuating and their size and configuration varying. The same statement declined to discuss impacts to operations or force protection measures, and noted only that the FAA had been made aware.

What that statement omitted was the scale of the response. Flight-tracking hobbyists watching Newport News in mid-December saw F-16s flying what looked like combat air patrols with tanker support around 12 December. The following week, one of NASA's three WB-57F high-altitude research jets, civil registration N927NA, flew circular orbits with Langley at their center. NASA's own public airborne-science calendar listed N927NA as tasked with 'Imagery Support' on 18 and 19 December 2023. Asked about it, NASA's Langley Research Center said the aircraft had been on the East Coast to image the SpaceX CRS-29 capsule's return and that 'while in the area, the aircraft provided additional imaging support in Virginia.' A NORAD/NORTHCOM spokesperson told The War Zone in December that NORTHCOM 'has been coordinating with [the] FBI' and referred further questions to the Bureau. The FBI declined to comment then and declined again in March 2024.

The senior officer on the ground was Gen. Mark Kelly, then commander of Air Combat Command, headquartered at Langley. He went to the roof of a squadron building for an unobstructed view. His account, given to 60 Minutes in March 2025, is the most detailed first-person military description on the record: 'The reports were coming in 20-to-30 sightings, same time every evening, 30-to-45 minutes after sunset.' The objects varied in size, altitude, and speed. 'The smallest, you know you're talking about a commercial-size quadcopter. And then the largest ones are probably size what I would call a bass boat or a small car.' The Wall Street Journal, reporting in October 2024, had one object at roughly twenty feet long, moving at more than 100 miles an hour at 3,000 to 4,000 feet, with others following one by one and sounding at distance like a parade of lawn mowers.

Gen. Glen VanHerck was the NORAD and NORTHCOM commander at the time. He provided fighters, AWACS, and helicopters to try to characterize the objects, and could not. NORAD's radars, built to see high-altitude bombers and missiles, could not see things a person could see with the naked eye. Asked by CBS whether he could rule out hobbyists, VanHerck said no: 'It would be my assessment they weren't hobbyists because of the magnitude of the events, the sizes of some of the drones, and the duration.' He added the sentence the board treats as load-bearing: 'It certainly could have a foreign nexus, a threat nexus.' A senior official in the Biden White House told 60 Minutes, anonymously, that it was likely the work of hobbyists. Both statements describe the same seventeen nights. Only one of them is attributable.

The first public official acknowledgment came on 14 March 2024, when VanHerck's successor, Gen. Gregory Guillot, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that counter-UAS had dominated his first month in command, that he 'wasn't prepared for the number of incursions,' and that he had 'gone into the events at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, and I'm using that as the centerpiece of my 90-day assessment.' The War Zone published its investigation the next day. Everything the public knows about Langley therefore entered the record either through a reporter's persistence or through a general's aside at a budget hearing, never through an announcement.

The subsequent posture is instructive. In October 2024 Guillot told reporters at Peterson Space Force Base that 'the only thing I can tell you about the Langley drones is roughly the number and roughly the altitude,' that he did not know whether they had been tracked to a recovery point or launched from a vessel offshore, and that he knew of no 'organized or unorganized foreign nexus.' That same month, Langley's 633rd Contracting Squadron posted a sources-sought notice for counter-drone netting to be draped over up to 42 open-ended aircraft sunshades: a base that could not identify what flew over it buying nets to catch it. In February 2025 Guillot told the SASC there had been 350 drone detections at 100 different military installations in 2024, and that only about half of U.S. installations even qualify as 'covered installations' with authority to act under 10 U.S.C. 130i.

Then came New Jersey. Beginning November 2024, thousands of sightings across the Northeast produced a joint DHS/FBI/FAA/DoD statement on 16 December 2024 asserting that the agencies had 'not identified anything anomalous.' The statement is the concealment posture in its purest form: an assurance issued about a phenomenon the same document concedes generated more than 5,000 tips and roughly 100 open leads. Langley is what that assurance is built on top of, and Langley was never solved.

VanHerck, retired and unconstrained, closed the loop in August 2026 at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium. 'There were no surprises, at least for myself and the team at NORAD/NORTHCOM and others,' he said of learning about the incursions. He had told Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin on 16 December 2021, two years to the week before Langley, that he lacked the domain awareness to do his mission, and that 'we're not set up to fight in and from our own land.' Installation commanders, he said, 'really felt a lack of trust' about whether they would be covered if they shot at something. The record therefore shows an air-defense system that knew it was blind, wrote it down, briefed it upward, and then watched seventeen nights of objects it could not name pass over its own F-22s.
openQuestions: No launch or recovery point was ever identified. Guillot stated in October 2024 that he did not know whether the objects were tracked to a recovery point or whether they could have been launched from a vessel offshore, leaving the maritime-launch hypothesis neither confirmed nor excluded.

On what basis were the objects classified as 'uncrewed aerial systems'? None was downed, captured, or attributed. The Air Force has never disclosed the identification methodology, and the 'UAS' label is the single act that removed the event from the anomaly-resolution track.

Why does AARO say it received no report when other reporting places AARO personnel in two weeks of interagency meetings on the incident? Either the office was excluded from a case squarely within its charter, or its public statement is incomplete. Both readings are consequential.

What did the NASA WB-57F N927NA record on 18-19 December 2023? No imagery, sensor tasking order, or product from those flights has been released, and NASA's public explanation attributes the deployment to a spacecraft-reentry imaging mission.

The FBI investigative file remains unreleased and the Bureau has declined comment continuously since December 2023. It is not publicly known whether the investigation was closed, and if so on what finding.

What did Langley's own counter-UAS equipment register? Security Forces are equipped with handheld Dronebuster-type detection and jamming devices, yet seventeen nights of activity produced no publicly acknowledged operator geolocation or radio-frequency signature.
Whether Gen. Guillot's 90-day NORAD/NORTHCOM assessment, of which Langley was the stated centerpiece, contains a Langley-specific annex, and whether any portion of it is releasable.

Civilian eyewitness Jonathan Butner described orb-shaped objects and a separate low-flying saucer-form object, and provided his video to the FBI. Whether any government entity analyzed that footage and what it concluded is unestablished; his morphological description and the official 'UAS' classification have never been reconciled.
Which specific F-22 airframes were relocated, to which base, and under whose order. The relocation is confirmed by 60 Minutes and VanHerck but no unit-level movement record has surfaced.

Whether the October 2023 drone overflights of the Energy Department's Nevada National Security Site, reported by the Wall Street Journal two months before Langley, are operationally connected to the Virginia events or merely contemporaneous.

Whether any classified session of the Senate or House Armed Services Committees produced a finding on Langley attribution, and whether such a finding, if it exists, differs from the public 'no known foreign nexus' posture Wicker's 'still mystified' remark implicitly denies.

Whether the F-16 combat air patrols observed over southeastern Virginia around 12 December 2023 were flown in direct response to the incursions, and whether any airborne sensor track of the objects exists from those sorties or from the AWACS and helicopter assets VanHerck says he provided.
dossier.whatItIs: A sustained wave of unidentified aerial incursions over Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Hampton, Virginia, beginning the evening of 6 December 2023 and running for roughly seventeen nights into late December. The objects overflew the home of the 1st Fighter Wing and the headquarters of Air Combat Command, the East Coast's principal F-22 Raptor base and a linchpin of the NORAD air-defense mission for Washington, D.C. Neither the Air Force, NORTHCOM, the FBI, nor the Pentagon's UAP office has ever publicly identified what the objects were, who operated them, or where they launched from.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the cleanest modern test case of the board's central proposition: that the United States government maintains a category of aerial object it will not name, and that its institutional response to encountering one is to reach for a label rather than an answer. For seventeen consecutive nights, objects that a four-star general watched from a rooftop transited restricted airspace over the most defended fighter base on the Atlantic seaboard, and the response was to move the F-22s, call in a NASA high-altitude imaging aircraft, hold two weeks of interagency meetings, and then say nothing for three months until a trade publication forced the acknowledgment. The objects were classified as 'uncrewed aerial systems' without a single one being downed, captured, tracked to a launch point, or attributed to any operator, and the Pentagon's own anomaly office told a reporter in May 2024 that it had never received a report on the incident at all. The government therefore produced, in the same event, a defense failure it could not explain and a taxonomy it could not justify: a 'drone' with no drone attached to it. Langley is the node where the concealment apparatus and the air-defense apparatus become visibly the same apparatus, because the thing that stopped the inquiry was not an absence of sensors but an official noun.

entityInfo.desc: The December 2023 Langley incursions are where the historical UAP record and the contemporary homeland-defence problem stop being separable. For at least seventeen nights beginning 6 December 2023, unidentified aircraft operated over a front-line F-22 base in Virginia. The response was not what an installation mounts against hobbyists: F-16 combat air patrols with tanker support, NASA's WB-57F high-altitude research aircraft flying surveillance orbits, FBI coordination routed through NORTHCOM. At least one object was described by Gen. Mark Kelly as roughly 20 feet long, moving at more than 100 mph at 3,000 to 4,000 feet. F-22s were moved; by October 2024 the Air Force was evaluating protective netting for the aircraft on the ground. And the commander of NORAD and US Northern Command, having made the incident the centrepiece of his 90-day assessment, said on the record that he knew of no organized or unorganized foreign nexus. The pattern then repeated and escalated: New Jersey in December 2024, met with a four-agency statement that resolved about 100 of more than 5,000 reports and generalised the result; UK bases in November 2024; a joint interagency task force in August 2025; an Inspector General finding in January 2026 that ten evaluated installations lacked coherent counter-drone authority; and in March 2026 waves of 12 to 15 jam-resistant drones over a nuclear-capable B-52 base during an active bombing campaign. Whatever these objects are, the record they generate is identical in shape to the record the 2004 and 2015 encounters generated: detected, tracked, unattributed, and officially minimised.
